title: The substructures within the pyramid
coreMove: Test every support set for vertical summary, horizontal sameness, and meaningful order before trusting the hierarchy.
sourcePressure: Chapter 2 narrows from why pyramids help to what makes the internal substructure stable: the point above must summarize, siblings must be logically alike, and sibling order must mean something.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Assuming parallel bullets or matching grammar make a real group when the lower points are doing different jobs.

sourceAnchors.name: horizontal relationship
sourceAnchors.detail: the sidecar says the heading index supports the horizontal relationship as a core subtopic for this chapter
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The horizontal relationship is the quiet test under a neat list: are these siblings, or only neighbors?

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective recognition, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm through a direct second-person passage, a short research/source aside, a reader question, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: a museum membership team revising reasons for a price increase
exampleSpecs.stakes: members may cancel if the rationale mixes costs, benefits, and apologies under one vague heading
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Hannah writes the job of each bullet in the margin, crosses out the apology bullet, and rebuilds the section as three cost pressures under one honest summary.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The membership letter smells faintly of toner and coffee when Hannah marks the margin.

exampleSpecs.domain: a railway safety officer grouping near-miss reports
exampleSpecs.audience: safety readers who need clean classes of evidence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a false group could send investigators toward training when track layout is the issue
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Antoine separates causes from locations and outcomes, then rewrites the parent line after the old one can no longer summarize the new sibling sets.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Rain taps the depot window while three near-miss forms sit under one bad heading.

exampleSpecs.domain: a cookbook editor organizing troubleshooting notes for sourdough bakers
exampleSpecs.stakes: home bakers will misdiagnose failures if ingredients, timing, and symptoms sit as one group
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sophie moves symptoms into one group and interventions into another, proving that the previous heading had been summarizing unlike items.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Sophie until the third loaf photo to see the list was lying.

exampleSpecs.domain: a cybersecurity compliance lead preparing audit findings
exampleSpecs.audience: risk officers who need findings that are the same kind
exampleSpecs.stakes: the board could fund the wrong fix if policy gaps, tool failures, and user habits are collapsed
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 9:10 a.m., David refuses to call all six findings controls, sorts them by policy, system, and behavior, and rewrites the summary to match only one set.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 9:10 a.m., David stares at six findings in a red audit binder.

exampleSpecs.domain: a vineyard operations planner summarizing harvest bottlenecks
exampleSpecs.audience: agricultural managers balancing field and cellar constraints
exampleSpecs.stakes: the harvest crew schedule will fail if weather, equipment, and staffing are treated as one timeline
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Margaux split weather risks from equipment constraints, then choose ranking order only inside the equipment group where one standard applies.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You can smell crushed grape skins while the bottleneck list hangs beside the crush pad.

exampleSpecs.domain: a university housing director explaining move-in problems
exampleSpecs.stakes: next year's fix depends on whether the problems are stages, causes, or resources
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ben says the list has three grammatically similar bullets but no shared class, then turns one false group into separate stage and resource groups.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "They look parallel, but they are not siblings," Ben says over the move-in map.

skillTargets: distinguish visual parallelism from logical parallelism
repair a mixed support group by separating functions
judge whether a top line overclaims its children
select an order that carries meaning rather than convenience

tryThisNowSpec: Take one three-bullet section and write one word beside each bullet naming its job, such as cause, action, risk, or result. If the words differ, split the group.
